source.title: Get rich quick: exact solutions reveal how unbalanced initializations promote rapid feature learning
source.authors: D. Kunin; Allan Ravent'os; C. Dominé; Feng Chen; D. Klindt; Andrew M. Saxe; Surya Ganguli

record.tranche_reason: Tests grokking on modular arithmetic with a changed intervention: it varies embedding initialization scale and measures steps to training and grokking thresholds.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports results on CNNs, CIFAR10, and hierarchical synthetic data, but these results concern feature learning, filter properties, accuracy, or sample complexity—not delayed generalization on those data. They are not rows for these claim versions. The grokking result is reported in Figure 12; the text gives its qualitative takeaway, while the plotted values are not available as extractable numbers.
record.test_reason: Trains a one-layer transformer on the Power et al. modular-arithmetic task. It sweeps embedding scale α and logit scale τ and reports steps to 99% train and 99% validation accuracy (Fig. 12). That bears on the delay (V1) and on initialization scale controlling it (V3).
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that decreasing the embedding variance (an upstream, unbalanced rich initialization; under 6% of parameters) significantly reduces time to grokking. They frame grokking as a lazy-to-rich transition, citing Kumar et al.
record.recipe_differences: Rather than reproducing the original grokking setup, the paper uses a single-layer transformer and varies embedding initialization scale and logit scale, reporting steps to accuracy thresholds.
record.method_sensitivity: Grokking time varies with embedding initialization scale; the experiment also sweeps logit scale τ with a compensating learning-rate change.

fits_no_version.finding: Upstream (small first-layer) initializations speed feature learning in CNNs, give smoother filters on CIFAR10, and lower sample complexity on the Random Hierarchy Model. No delayed-generalization measure is reported.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Relative layer-wise initialization scale (upstream vs downstream) controls the speed of rich feature learning in finite-width networks.

record.problems: The grokking result is plotted rather than tabulated, so individual values and uncertainty are not extractable. The experiment averages over 5 random initializations and has a maximum computational budget of 30,000 training steps.

untested.parts: Dependence of the delay on training-set size; full accuracy trajectories showing chance-level test accuracy before the jump.

Grokking-like delays on non-algorithmic data (the CNN/CIFAR10, MNIST and RHM experiments measure feature learning, filter smoothness and sample complexity, not delayed generalization). Whether the delay can be fully switched off, rather than shortened.

missing.what: Colorbar ranges of Fig. 12: train-threshold steps about 30–75; grok-threshold steps 0–2.4e4. Together these quantify the train/test delay.
Whether any (α,τ) cells failed to grok within the 30,000-step budget is not stated.

record.verdict_notes: The grokking experiment is a small appendix demonstration within a theory paper on lazy/rich learning. Verdicts rest on figure colorbars and the authors' qualitative statement, not on tabulated values. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test how delay changes with training-set size, or report an accuracy trajectory establishing chance-level test accuracy after perfect training accuracy followed by a near-perfect jump.
The non-algorithmic experiments do not test grokking-like delayed generalization on those data.

rows.subject: one layer transformer model
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular arithmetic while varying embedding initialization scale; also scale logits by τ and divide the learning rate by τ².

conditions.value: modular arithmetic task in Power et al. [68]

rows.measure: Training steps until training accuracy passes 99%
rows.note: The figure reports this threshold measure across the stated sweep, but its values cannot be extracted here. This measure alone does not establish the delay between training and generalization.
rows.check: Per-cell values are not readable. The Fig. 12(a) colorbar spans about 3.0e+01 to 7.5e+01 steps, so training saturates within tens of steps. Alone it cannot show the delay, but it is the baseline against which R2 shows one.

rows.subject: one layer transformer model
rows.operation_detail: Train on modular arithmetic while varying embedding initialization scale; also scale logits by τ and divide the learning rate by τ².

conditions.value: modular arithmetic task in Power et al. [68]

rows.measure: Training steps until validation accuracy reaches at least 99% (caption describes this as test performance)
rows.note: The authors state that grokking is fastest in an unbalanced rich setting and that decreasing embedding variance significantly reduces time to grokking. The figure's individual values are not extractable.
rows.check: The Fig. 12(b) colorbar spans 0 to 2.4e+04 steps versus tens of steps to fit training data, so generalization lags memorization by orders of magnitude in at least some cells. Time to grok varies strongly with α and τ: authors report the fastest grokking in the unbalanced rich setting. Bears on V3's initialization-scale part as well as V1. Values per cell are not extractable.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix D.3, Grokking; Figure 12(b) and caption.

relationships.condition: One-layer transformer, modular arithmetic, α∈{0.1..10}, τ∈{0.5..1.5}, 5 seeds, 30k-step budget
relationships.reason: Training reaches 99% within about 30–75 steps (R1 colorbar) while validation 99% takes up to about 2.4e4 steps (R2 colorbar), a large delay. Based on figure colorbars only.
relationships.display_finding: Training reached 99% accuracy within approximately 30–75 steps, while validation took up to approximately 24,000 steps to reach 99%.

relationships.condition: Initialization-scale manipulation on modular arithmetic only (relative embedding scale α plus Kumar-style logit scale τ)
relationships.reason: Time to grok shifts strongly with initialization scale. It is shortest in the unbalanced rich (small-embedding) setting, consistent with a lazy-to-rich account (R2). The control comes through relative layer scale, not only overall scale.
relationships.display_finding: Grokking occurred fastest with small embeddings in the unbalanced rich regime, showing strong dependence on relative layer initialization scales.

relation.reason: The study measures training and validation accuracy threshold times under initialization manipulations.

tranche.reason: A single-layer transformer initialization sweep tests grokking timing through relative embedding and output scaling.

source_check.notes: Figure 12 supplies colorbar scales but no numerical cell values. Embeddings are divided by α, so larger α means smaller embeddings; the authors' reduced-variance conclusion is supported.

statements.correction: Positional and token embedding weights divided by α; logits multiplied by τ; learning rate divided by τ²; fastest grokking in an unbalanced rich setting; total parameter norm not controlled.
statements.problem: Relative embedding scale affects grokking time, but the experiment does not hold total parameter norm fixed or isolate an effect beyond total norm.
